Project ID: Project 16- Alan Wing- 63- "Stochastic resonance in touch for pe..."
Project title: Stochastic resonance in touch for perception and action (STRITPA2)
Project summary:
Sensations from the hands and feet are fundamental to the way we perceive and interact with our environment. Touch receptors transmit afferent information to the brain via neural activity in peripheral nerves and the spinal cord, providing critical information about physical contact. When this transmission is disrupted, by aging or through disorders such as peripheral neuropathy, both perception and control of action are affected. Basic sensory experiences such as tactile detection and discrimination in the hand and foot can be impaired, and actions such as grasping and maintaining balance compromised.
Recent studies have consistently shown that adding random vibration (“noise”) at sub-threshold levels can enhance the detection and transmission of weak tactile signals (through a process sometimes referred to as “stochastic resonance”), and thus improve balance and hand function1. For example, sub-threshold vibration delivered at the wrist has been shown to benefit fingertip tactile detection2, suggesting the potential utility of a vibrating wrist band for stroke rehabilitation3. Sub-threshold wrist vibration has also been shown to benefit individuals with chemotherapy induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN)4. Random noise at 60% detection thresholds presented at the wrist improved detection of tactile events at the fingertip compared with when wrist vibration was absent or presented at 120% detection thresholds. Moreover, finger movements driving hand aperture during reaching exhibited reduced normalized jerk (see Fig1), suggesting improved kinesthesis (combining proprioception and tactile sensation).
Vibration at the wrist is likely to be transmitted to and excite mechanoreceptors throughout the hand5. This activation is believed to underlie improvements observed in somatosensory function with sub-threshold vibration. The proposed project aims to:
(i) Extend the approach of Osumi et al4, testing the effects of wrist vibration in healthy older adults or people with chemotherapy induced peripheral neuropathy (due to cancer treatment) across a range of behavioural measures of passive and active fingertip touch function;
(ii) Computationally examine the origins of wrist vibration benefits by simulating vibration effects on the population of touch afferents in the hand. This will be accomplished using TouchSim6, developed by Saal et aal and previously successfully used by Wing et al to account for age-based decline in 2-point discrimination threshold7.

Project ID: Project 17- Alan Wing- 63- "Tactile control of in-hand manipulat..."
Project title: Tactile control of in-hand manipulation
Project summary:
This MSc project will investigate the sensorimotor mechanisms underlying voluntary object rotation within a precision grip. The task will model a familiar everyday action such as picking up a pencil from a table with surface normal grip force generated by the thumb and index finger coordinated with lift (tangential load) force from the arm and then rotating it into a preferred writing orientation, using force generated by the middle finger to create a destabilising torque that is controlled in conjunction with the normal grip force. Participants will perform a series of controlled object-rotation movements while thumb – index finger forces, middle finger generated torques, and object kinematics (rotation) are recorded to examine how the nervous system coordinates manipulation and stability during dexterous hand actions.

The project builds on the torque stabilisation framework developed by Wing and Lederman (1998), which demonstrated how the digits coordinate force and torque production to maintain stable object orientation during precision grip. A central aim will be to distinguish the contributions of feedforward and feedback control by manipulating both frictional conditions (dry versus wet fingertips) and the quality of somatosensory input (bare fingers, single surgical gloves, and double surgical gloves). These manipulations are expected to alter both the frictional coupling between the digits and the object and the availability of tactile feedback, thereby changing the balance between anticipatory control and online correction.

The work is further motivated by recent evidence that sensory impairment compromises dexterous manipulation, including findings from Roberts et al. (2025) demonstrating deficits in precision grip control in individuals with chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN). By identifying how sensory and mechanical factors influence rotational stability during within-hand manipulation, the project will advance understanding of skilled hand function and provide a foundation for future investigations of dexterity impairments associated with sensory loss, ageing, and neurological conditions. More broadly, the study may provide a quantitative and mechanistically grounded complement to in-hand manipulation assessment tools such as those reviewed by Pont et al (2009) and being developed by Liu and colleagues (2018, 2025), helping to link clinical measures of manual dexterity with the underlying sensorimotor processes that support skilled object manipulation.

Project ID: Project 38- Andrea Krott- 77- "The relationship of Theory of Mind, ..."
Project title: The relationship of Theory of Mind, cognition and language skills in monolingual and bilingual children
Project summary: Theory of Mind (ToM) is the ability to attribute mental states (e.g., beliefs desires, and emotions) to others to predict or explain their behaviour. Various studies have examined the association between ToM development and development of other cognitive functions, for instance meta-linguistic awareness (MLA). The latter the conscious reflection on the structural features of language (e.g., sounds, morphological units, and syntactic structures), treating language forms as objects of thought rather than focusing on their communicative meaning. Both MLA and ToM undergo substantial growth during early and middle childhood, and both require children to step back from a dominant perspective and think about abstract representations, whether linguistic or mental. But the relationship between ToM and MLA as well as its relationship with wider cognitive skills remains unclear. In addition, the relationship appears to be affected by children's experience with more than one language. The current project therefore investigates relationships between ToM, MLA and cognition within monolingual and bilingual children (~3-5 year olds).

Project ID: Project 12- Andrew Bagshaw- 58- "Examining brain state variability wi..."
Project title: Examining brain state variability with fNIRS and fMRI
Project summary: The majority of the brain’s physiological and metabolic activity is concerned with intrinsic processes, not responses to external stimulation. Even robust sensory stimuli lead to relatively minor perturbations to the system, as the brain constantly adapts its processing to meet instantaneous and competing internal, environmental and behavioural demands. This observation rarely features in neuroimaging analyses, which erroneously assume a dissociation between stimulus responses and ongoing brain activity. The consequence of this is that the majority of the signal is considered to be noise and rejected, which could be a significant contributing factor to why functional neuroimaging of individual participants is not considered robust. Functional variability is not noise: a considerable proportion of it can be explained by the dynamics of ongoing brain activity, or ‘brain state’, and it is predictive of behaviour, pathology and development through the lifespan. This project will work with existing projects acquiring functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and functional MRI (fMRI) data and examine signal variability, with a particular application to the relationship with ADHD and sleep traits.

Project ID: Project 35- Andrew Quinn- 76- "Do OPMs tell us more about brain act..."
Project title: Do OPMs tell us more about brain activity than EEG?
Project summary:
Neuroimaging technologies are progressing quickly at the moment, Optically Pumped Magnetometers are an exciting new technology for Magnetoencephalography that promises to revolutionise our understanding of the brain. However, it is challenging to compare to existing methods like EEG and we often end up just making indirect comparisons or relying on assumptions that OPMs are better 'in theory'.

This project will work with a rare dataset that acquired simultaneous EEG-OPM from participants during a variety of tasks. This will allow us to track the information recorded by each modality from identical underlying brain sources. Analysis of this dataset allows us to compare what aspects of brain function are captured by each. We can use this to quantify the benefit of emerging OPM technologies for quantifying critical but challenging features such as bursting dynamics and waveform shape.

There is flexibility about the specific analysis and members of the group can collaborate on data processing but work towards personal goals, I'm happy to discuss specific ideas or pitches prior to the project - just get in touch.

This is a data-analysis focused project that will make use of existing open-access data though there may be opportunities to gain exposure to the EEG and OPM labs. This project will have proportionally more time for analysis and coding than projects involving data collection and there is an expectation that our analysis will be explored in considerable detail.

The project will suit people looking to strengthen their understanding of neuronal oscillations, data-science, statistics and Python coding. Some prior experience and interest in these topics will be required.

Project ID: Project 61- Andrew Surtees- 88- "Measuring Experiences of the Double ..."
Project title: Measuring Experiences of the Double Empathy Problem
Project summary: Empathy is the ability to understand and feel the emotions of other people. Autistic people are often characterised as having less empathy for others, and regularly score lower on traditional measures of empathy. Milton (2012) highlighted how a breakdown in mutual understanding (an empathy "error") occurs across a dyad (not within an individual), and that this is more likely in pairs of people with a greater disparity in their native communication and interaction dispositions. As such, empathy problems are not problems "for" autistic people, but rather for autistic and non-autistic dyads. One corrollary of this is that (as a neurominority), autistic people should not only have regular experiences of struggling to understand and feel the emotions of others, but also of feeling misunderstood or "unfelt" by others. Qualtative work suggests this is the case, however, there are few quantitative ways to measure this. This project will convert existing questionnaire measures of empathy to measuring the experience of empathy felt from others, examine their psychometric properties and correlates in autistic and non-autistic participants.
Topic: Empathy, Autism
Methodology: Questionnaire

Project ID: Project 62- Anke Buttner- 80- "What helps make for a good second ye..."
Project title: What helps make for a good second year at University?
Project summary:
Much of the institutional efforts in supporting UK undergraduate students are focused on the first year of study with its transition to university (with retention an important metric) and on the final year of study in which students complete their individual projects and are getting ready for the next step in their careers (with employment statistics and the National Student Survey – NSS as measures of success for the institution). The second year of study, however, brings its own challenges: there is a step up in academic demands, grades start to count towards the final degree classification, and many students will be living in shared houses with their friends for the first time. There is documented evidence of ‘second year blues’ in the UK (e.g. Jacobs & Newstead, 2000), and of an equivalent ‘sophomore slump’ in the US (e.g. Pattengale & Schreiner, 2000). The aim of this project is to explore the experiences of second year students in Higher Education with a view to understanding the specific challenges faced by students in the ‘forgotten year’ and going forward to develop resources to support the transition to and experience of the second year on undergraduate programmes. Project ID: Project 48- Anna Kowalczyk- 46- "Improving Co-registration Methods fo..."
Project title: Improving Co-registration Methods for OPM-MEG Neuroimaging
Project summary:
Co-registration is the process of aligning data from different sources into a single coordinate system. In MEG (magnetoencephalography), this involves aligning sensor positions with anatomical images from MRI scans to ensure that brain activity is accurately mapped to the participant’s brain surface. Optically Pumped Magnetometers (OPMs) offer a modern, flexible alternative to traditional MEG systems. Our OPM-MEG system uses an array of sensors embedded in a smart helmet, which adjusts to the participant's head shape and automatically tracks sensor positions.
Traditionally, co-registration relies on digitizing head shapes using tools like the Polhemus tracker and aligning sensor positions with MRI data through anatomical landmarks. However, new technologies, such as smart helmets and smartphone-based 3D scanning apps, provide alternative methods for co-registration.
Recently, we have developed a dedicated co-registration graphical user interface (GUI) that facilitates the use of 3D head scans for OPM-MEG co-registration. This project offers an opportunity to help shape the next stages of this development and explore future directions for improving co-registration workflows. Depending on your interests and skill set, possible project directions include testing and validating the GUI using existing OPM-MEG datasets, learning about source reconstruction methods, and comparing the performance of different co-registration approaches based on Polhemus digitization, smart helmet sensor localization, and 3D scan-derived head surfaces. There may also be opportunities to assist with pilot OPM-MEG data collections and apply these methods to newly acquired datasets. Alternatively, students with strong Python programming skills and experience working with GitHub-managed projects can contribute directly to the ongoing development of the GUI by implementing new features and improving its functionality. Through these activities, the project will contribute to advancing practical, accurate, and user-friendly co-registration solutions for OPM-MEG research.

Project ID: Project 67- Cathy Manning- 93- "Visual discomfort in autistic and no..."
Project title: Visual discomfort in autistic and non-autistic children and adults
Project summary:
Autistic people commonly experience differences in sensory processing which can negatively affect quality of life and mental health. In particular, heightened reactivity to sensory information can result in discomfort, which can make certain spaces and activities (like attending medical settings) disabling. There is a widespread recognition that we need to make spaces and services more sensory-inclusive for autistic people, as reflected in policy and initiatives like quiet hours. However, there is very little information about how to adapt sensory information to make it more comfortable for autistic individuals, without adversely affecting others.

This project will begin to provide this necessary information. We will systematically find out the precise sensory parameters that lead to visual discomfort in autistic participants, and whether this differs from typically developing individuals. We focus on the visual system as heightened visual reactivity in autism is currently poorly characterised, yet there is a well-established literature characterising visual discomfort in non-autistic populations which we can draw upon. The project aims to uncover the general stimulus features underlying visual discomfort in autistic individuals, while taking account of individual differences. This will give a more precise characterisation of visual discomfort in autism, which will in turn allow us to uncover the underlying mechanisms.

We will work with a group of consultants with lived experience (e.g., autistic individuals and parents of autistic children) to guide the project. In the first part of the project, we will present autistic and typically developing children and adults with a range of visual stimuli (including striped patterns, flickering videos and natural images), either in-person or online, and participants will rate how uncomfortable they are. We will also see whether discomfort ratings relate to self-report and parent-report questionnaires, to make links with everyday life and to help begin to understand why discomfort ratings might vary from person-to-person. In the second part of the project, we will take the most and least comfortable stimuli for autistic children and use these to link discomfort to brain activation using EEG (a technique which measures electrical activity at the scalp) and measures of arousal including heart-rate and pupil size. These links will help us understand why autistic children experience more visual discomfort than typically developing children.

The project will precisely characterise heightened reactivity to visual information in autism and identify underlying mechanisms. The findings will inform how environments (e.g., patterns of carpets, building frontages) and visual materials (e.g., educational resources, websites) should be designed or adapted to minimise discomfort for autistic people. By minimising the uncomfortable stimuli that autistic individuals are exposed to, we have the potential to improve mental health and quality of life for autistic individuals. By additionally studying physiological mechanisms, we can link the sensory symptoms experienced by autistic people with underlying physiology, and may be able to develop nonverbal measures of discomfort which could ultimately be used with autistic individuals with few-to-no words.
Topic: autism; development; sensory; child; EEG; cognitive neuroscience; psychophysiology
Methodology: There are both in-person and online parts of this project, which students would be welcome to choose between, in discussion with the supervisor. In-person: we are seeing autistic and non-autistic children aged 6-14 years and finding out what they find comfortable or uncomfortable, and why. Children give visual discomfort ratings, and we will measure EEG and autonomic (ECG, pupillometry) responses. We are also seeing autistic and non-autistic adults, to compare which stimuli they find comfortable or uncomfortable to look at. Online: autistic and non-autistic adults and children judge whether a range of natural images are "comfortable" or "uncomfortable". We will then use image statistics (e.g., spatial frequency information, colour contrasts) to see if we can predict which images they find comfortable or not, and whether these predictions vary across autistic and non-autistic participants.

Project ID: Project 30- Clare Anderson- 69- "Characterizing the First Night Effec..."
Project title: Characterizing the First Night Effect in Human Sleep with Quantitative EEG (qEEG) Markers
Project summary:
This project focuses on the first night effect, a well-recognized phenomenon in sleep research in which a person’s first night in a sleep laboratory differs from subsequent nights because of the unfamiliar environment, monitoring equipment, or anticipatory stress. These adaptation-related changes can affect both subjective sleep experience and objective sleep measures, potentially influencing the interpretation of laboratory sleep recordings.

The study will examine the first night effect using quantitative EEG (qEEG) markers, allowing a more detailed assessment of brain activity than standard sleep-stage scoring alone. By looking more closely at EEG dynamics, the project aims to identify subtle changes in cortical arousal, sleep stability, spectral power, and other neurophysiological features that may not be captured by conventional analyses.

The project will have the opportunity to explore these effects across the full sleep laboratory experience, including the pre-sleep period, during sleep, and post-sleep during the morning wake period. There is also potential to further explore individual differences in the first night effect including age, personality traits, chronotype or baseline sleep characteristics.
Topic: Sleep, EEG, first night effect, age
Methodology: This is a pre-existing dataset.   The student will have access to data from healthy participants who have completed at least two overnight sleep laboratory recordings, enabling comparison between the initial laboratory night and a subsequent night. Polysomnographic data have been collected throughout the stay in addition to next day alertness and vigilance testing. Detailed quantitative EEG (qEEG) analyses will be used to assess changes in brain activity beyond standard sleep-stage scoring (which is already available). qEEG markers can be examined during the pre-sleep, intra-sleep, and post-sleep periods to capture anticipatory arousal, sleep microstructure, and any residual morning effects. This markers may include aperiodic signals, graph metrics, local sleep and other qEEG markers. Measures of individual differences, including trait anxiety, habitual sleep quality, and age, are available as predictors of response.

Understanding how different patterns of social media use relate to young people’s wellbeing and social functioning is particularly important, given that early adolescence represents a critical developmental period characterised by substantial social and emotional change.

These analytical skills are highly valued by employers and provide an excellent foundation for students considering further postgraduate research, including PhD study.
This project is particularly suitable for students interested in understanding how digital environments shape young people’s development and wellbeing, and who wish to contribute to evidence that can inform educational, clinical, and policy initiatives aimed at promoting healthy digital engagement among adolescents.

Project ID: Project 5- Jonathan Lee- 50- "Effortful reminder and memory recons..."
Project title: Effortful reminder and memory reconsolidation
Project summary: Reminder of previously-learned information can engage a process of memory destabilisation-reconsolidation. Project ID: Project 20- Katia Vione- 66- "Thinking, Believing, and Deciding: C..."
Project title: Thinking, Believing, and Deciding: Cognitive and Personality Predictors of Misinformation Susceptibility
Project summary:
The proliferation of misinformation — false or misleading content presented as factual — has been identified as a significant public health and social concern, with documented consequences for vaccination uptake, political behaviour, and intergroup relations (Lewandowsky et al., 2017; Pennycook & Rand, 2021). Understanding who is susceptible to misinformation, and why, has therefore become a major priority for cognitive, social, and personality psychology. Despite a rapidly growing empirical literature, key theoretical questions remain unresolved. Does analytical thinking ability offer genuine protection against false belief, or does the motivation to think analytically matter just as much? Do personality traits predict misinformation susceptibility directly, or is their influence channelled through self-regulatory mechanisms such as metacognition and self-control? Remarkably, few studies have tested these questions within an integrative framework that considers cognitive ability, cognitive style, personality, and epistemic beliefs simultaneously. The overarching aim of this project is to examine the cognitive and personality predictors of susceptibility to misinformation, with particular attention to the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which these individual differences operate.

The project uses existing data from two large-scale online surveys collected in 2021 and 2022, with over 900 participants in each dataset prior to cleaning (approximately 500–600 usable responses per dataset following exclusions). Data were collected internationally, resulting in heterogeneous samples spanning multiple nationalities, educational backgrounds, and occupations. The datasets include validated measures of analytical thinking ability (Cognitive Reflection Test), cognitive motivation (Need for Cognition), critical thinking dispositions, metacognitive awareness, self-control, Big Five personality traits, conspiracist beliefs, and beliefs about the role of cognition in emotion regulation, as well as two measures of fake news belief and endorsement spanning health, social, political, and environmental misinformation topics. Demographic information is also available, including age, gender, educational level, occupation, nationality, and daily internet use.

This project will suit students who are interested in cognitive psychology, social psychology, and the psychology of belief. It is particularly relevant to those who wish to develop advanced quantitative data analysis skills, including moderation and mediation analysis using regression-based methods (e.g., Hayes' PROCESS macro). The ability to conduct and interpret these analyses is increasingly valued by employers and is especially important for those considering further academic research, including doctoral study. Students will receive guidance and support from the project supervisor as they develop these skills, and are expected to engage critically with the psychometric properties of the measures, the cross-sectional nature of the data, and the implications of a global convenience sample for the reliability and generalisability of their findings.

Project ID: Project 44- Katja Kornysheva- 81- "Generalisation of movement sequence ..."
Project title: Generalisation of movement sequence planning across movement types
Project summary:
Sequential movements such as handwriting and typing are prominently present in everyday life. These movements typically involve a set of separate movement elements that the brain needs to execute in quick succession. It remains unclear how the central nervous system can plan and perform such movement elements so seemingly effortlessly. To address this, there is a longstanding debate in neuromotor control on what the brain considers as a movement. Does the brain break down a movement into separate elements or does the brain essentially fuse these different elements into a single ‘holistic’ action? Fusing the different movement elements into a single holistic movement would require the brain to chunk the elements into a new neural representation.
Once sequential movements become overtrained (and can be retrieved from memory), the brain may start treating multiple movement elements as one. This is known as fusion and can happen at the behavioural and neural level. Whilst it is relatively well established that humans can fuse movement elements behaviourally, less is known about neural fusion. In fact, most research suggests that there is an absence of neural fusion. This is mostly backed up by primate literature. In a landmark study in 2021, Zimnik and Churchland showed that primates who had to perform single and double reaching movements, neuronal activity of the brain's motor areas is not different for both movements, suggesting that neural fusion does not happen. One criticism of this paper is that the two reaching movements were very similar, meaning that the absence of neural fusion could be the result of behavioural transfer. Instead, one should therefore pick two sequential movements in which this should not occur by essentially maximising the behavioural differences between the two movements.
The current MSc project will comprise the collection and analysis of electro-encephalographic (EEG) data. The analysis will particularly focus on how similar these two movements are prepared by the brain. This will involve analysing the EEG data using multivariate pattern analysis (e.g., competitive queueing [Kornysheva et al., 2019] and representational similarity analysis).

Methodology: MEG/ EEG, multivariate pattern analysis

Project ID: Project 63- Lei Zhang- 90- "What Does AI Think of Me? How AI-Gen..."
Project title: What Does AI Think of Me? How AI-Generated Feedback Shapes Self-Beliefs
Project summary:
From asking ChatGPT whether an email sounds rude, to seeking advice about restaurant recommendations and career choices, people are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence (AI) not just for information, but also for feedback about themselves. As AI becomes more personalised and conversational, an important question is whether its evaluations can actually shape how we see ourselves (i.e., Self belief).

Research in cognitive psychology has shown that people continuously form and revise beliefs about their own abilities based on feedback from others. However, this process is often biased: we may give more weight to feedback that confirms what we already believe, while discounting information that challenges our existing self-view. But what happens when that feedback comes from AI rather than another person? How about when the AI is more generic vs more personalised? Do we trust it less because “it is only an algorithm”, or more because AI can appear objective, knowledgeable, and unbiased?

In this project, the student will use an experimental task in which participants receive positive and negative evaluations of their abilities from either an AI system or a human evaluator. We will examine how these evaluations influence self-beliefs over time, and whether AI changes the way people respond to confirming versus conflicting feedback. Alongside behavioural analysis, the project can use computational modelling to estimate how strongly people learn from different types of feedback and whether these learning processes differ for AI and human sources. This project offers a timely way to study how AI may increasingly shape everyday self-perception and decision-making.

Project ID: Project 28- Magda Chechlacz- 68- "Exploring structural markers of brai..."
Project title: Exploring structural markers of brain and cognitive decline in association with modifiable lifestyle factors (e.g. sleep, education)
Project summary:
Numerous studies indicate large inter-individual differences in cognitive ageing, specifically in susceptibility to age-related cognitive decline (normal healthy ageing) and to disease-related pathology (dementia) or mental health problems. With an increasingly ageing world population, the key research challenges include understanding factors supporting maintenance of cognitive functioning in old age (good sleep, physical activity, education etc) and uncovering brain markers associated with high risk of cognitive decline and mental health problems in elderly population. The age-related cognitive decline is known to be associated with changes within neuronal networks, including altered structural connectivity, brain atrophy within various cortical and subcortical areas, cerebrovascular changes and functional networks dynamics. Increasing evidence suggests that lifetime cognitive stimulation compensates for age-related brain changes and accounts for differences in age-related cognitive decline. On the other hand, changes in sleep patterns/sleep loss (common complaint in older adults) contribute to age-related cognitive decline and affect mental health. The MSc project will offer opportunity to use advanced magnetic resonance imaging techniques (e.g., diffusion MRI based measures of connectivity, brain age estimation, cortical and subcortical parcellations, volumetric analysis) to explore brain ageing and to gain insights into potential factors underlying heterogeneity in cognitive ageing. Project ID: Project 25- Massimiliano Di Luca- 61- "From Papers to Evidence: Can AI Buil..."
Project title: From Papers to Evidence: Can AI Build a Reliable Research Vault?
Project summary: Research databases such as Locomotion Vault and the Text Entry for XR Trove demonstrate how structured collections of publications and techniques can reveal patterns that are difficult to identify through conventional narrative reviews. However, constructing these databases manually requires substantial expert time. This project will develop and evaluate an AI-assisted tool that identifies publications within a focused area of XR research, initially virtual-hand and embodied interaction, and converts them into a structured, traceable database. The tool will extract bibliographic information, study characteristics, participant numbers, interaction techniques, experimental conditions, outcome measures and numerical results. Every extracted value must be linked to supporting text or tables in the original publication. A manually coded subset will provide a gold-standard benchmark. The student will measure retrieval recall, extraction precision, accuracy, hallucination rate, processing cost and time saved. After validation, the resulting dataset will be used to test a preregistered research hypothesis, such as whether embodied hand input or multimodal feedback predicts improved performance, workload or user experience in XR. The central question is whether AI output is sufficiently accurate, reproducible and transparent to support valid scientific inference.
Topic: Artificial intelligence; data science; large language models; scientific information extraction; literature mining; evidence synthesis; research databases; extended reality; reproducible research
Methodology: Quantitative computational project. First, the student will define a focused XR domain, inclusion criteria and structured extraction schema. A reproducible pipeline will then discover publications, deduplicate records, screen them for eligibility and extract structured information with source-level provenance. A stratified subset will be manually coded and independently checked to form a gold-standard benchmark. AI outputs will be evaluated using retrieval recall, precision, F1 score, field-level accuracy, numerical error, unsupported-claim rate, processing cost and time. One substantive XR hypothesis will then be preregistered and tested using only fields that meet predetermined reliability thresholds. Sensitivity analyses will compare conclusions based on AI-extracted and human-verified data. The system will retain publication identifiers, supporting source passages, confidence values and processing logs.

Project ID: Project 15- Matthew Apps- 62- "Understanding the dynamics of fatigu..."
Project title: Understanding the dynamics of fatigue in health and neurological disease.
Project summary:
Fatigue -a pervasive feeling of exhaustion - is a sensation we are all familiar with. However, in many neurological conditions such as Parkinson's Disease and Multiple Sclerosis, feelings of fatigue can become severe and pervasive, significantly impairing daily life. Yet, relative to many other symptoms in neurology, we know very little about what in the brain and body underlies the symptom of fatigue. Recently, research led by the supervisor has begun to characterise moment-to-moment how fatigue rises and falls during demanding tasks, developing experimental tools that can precisely measure for each individual how rapidly fatigue builds up, and how quickly it subsides through rest.

The aim of this project will be to develop a new experiment that measures how much exerting effort, or taking rests, impacts on sensations of fatigue, and the degree to which it modulates levels of motivation. We will then use computational modelling to unpack the brain mechanisms underlying changes in fatigue and motivation and to quantify variability between people to test its association with levels of fatigue in daily life in the healthy population. By developing this new approach, it will provide a platform for testing how fatigue fluctuates in neurological disorders.

Methodology: Behavioural testing and computational modelling

Project ID: Project 18- Matthew Apps- 62- "Understanding the computations under..."
Project title: Understanding the computations underlying competitive effort.
Project summary: From beating your friends while gaming, to entering a writing competition, everyday we engage in social interactions where we compete with others. Research examining competition has often used economic games to understand the cognitive processes underlying how motivated people are when competing with others. In such experiments people are often competing on single trials to beat a single other opponent. Yet, while useful, such an approach misses many things that happens when we compete in the real world. For instance, when racing against others in a ParkRun, or several of our friends on Mario Kart or Gran Turismo, many other computations might impact on how motivated we are to engage in the competition. For instance, the competitions occurs over extended periods of time, rather than being a single-shot effort, during which motivation might fluctuate considerably. Moreover, If we are behind an opponent we might work harder to get in front, compared to if they are miles ahead of us, and we might be more motivated when competing with a smaller number of people than a large group. However, little research has been conducted that offers a an account of the computations that people engage in when motivating themselves during a competition that occurs over an extended period of time against multiple opponents. In this project the student will work with Prof. Apps and Dr. Hikaru Sugimoto, using an experimental task in which people have to make decisions about how much physical effort to exert when competing against other opponents in a race. Using computational modelling we will dissect the cognitive mechanisms that underlie competition and how they impact on the motivation to exert effort. This project will offer a unique perspective on the psychology of competition.
Topic: Competition; Effort; Motivation; Computation
Methodology: The project will involve behavioural experiments in-person and computational modelling.

Project ID: Project 57- Melissa Colloff- 87- "What Makes AI-Generated Faces Look R..."
Project title: What Makes AI-Generated Faces Look Real? Investigating the Role of Spatial Frequency in Human Perception
Project summary:
AI-generated faces have become remarkably realistic. People now struggle to distinguish AI-generated faces from photographs of real people and, strikingly, AI-generated faces can sometimes be perceived as more real than genuine faces—a phenomenon known as AI hyper-realism. But what visual information leads us to perceive an AI-generated face as real?
This project will investigate one potential mechanism: spatial-frequency information. The human visual system processes images at different spatial frequencies, which capture different levels of visual detail. Face recognition relies particularly strongly on information within certain spatial-frequency ranges. Interestingly, AI-generated images can contain subtle abnormalities in the distribution of information across these frequencies. Machine-learning systems can exploit these frequency-domain signatures to distinguish real from AI-generated images, but it remains unclear whether they also influence human perceptions of facial realness.

The project will investigate whether spatial-frequency characteristics associated with AI-generated faces help explain why some artificial faces appear so convincing. First, the student will conduct image analyses comparing the spatial-frequency properties of real and AI-generated faces. These findings will then inform manipulations of real facial images, allowing us to experimentally alter their spatial-frequency properties to more closely resemble those found in AI-generated faces. In an online behavioural experiment, participants will judge whether faces are real or AI-generated, allowing us to test whether manipulating this visual information systematically changes perceptions of realness.

The student will join an established research project and team of researchers (including Kyra Scott (https://www.appliedmemorylab.co.uk/kyra-scott), Prof Howard Bowman, and external collaborators) and will work with an existing experimental paradigm; all programming required for the online experiment has already been completed. The project therefore provides an opportunity to develop skills in face perception, experimental psychology, image analysis, online behavioural research and quantitative data analysis, while addressing a timely question at the intersection of human perception and artificial intelligence. It is anticipated that this work will be published.
Topic: Face Processing and Perception; Artificial Intelligence; Deepfake Detection; Decision-Making
Methodology: Behavioural Experiments; Image Analysis; Online Research

Project ID: Project 39- Paul Muhle-Karbe- 78- "Dissociating neural pathways for sel..."
Project title: Dissociating neural pathways for selective attention
Project summary:
Selective attention enables us to focus on goal-relevant information in the environment, while discarding irrelevant distraction. It is thought to rely upon top-down signals that are generated in the prefrontal cortex and amplify processing of goal-relevant information in sensory cortex. While this general framework is widely appreciated, the mechanisms by which attention biases perception are poorly understood.

Recent neuroimaging studies suggest that different forms of attention may utilise distinct neural pathways that connect unique sub-regions of the prefrontal cortex and the visual system: spatial attention may rely upon top-down signals from the frontal eye-field (FEF) that the dorsal visual stream, whereas non-spatial attention may rely upon top-down signals from the inferior frontal junction (IFJ) that target the ventral visual stream. This project seeks to put this hypothesis to a rigorous causal test using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) as a tool to transiently perturb these putative pathways.
Topic: selective attention, prefrontal cortex, brain stimulation, psychophysics
Methodology:
Participants perform computerised tasks requiring spatial and non-spatial forms of selective attention, while FEF, IFJ, and a control region are stimulated in different sessions using a theta-burst protocol that is known to transiently reduce neuronal excitability. Examining the disruptive effects of TMS as a function of task demand and targeted brain region will provide unprecedented insights into the functional neuroanatomy of selective attention.

Overall, the project’s findings will significantly enhance our understanding of attention and its impact on neuropsychiatric conditions. Additionally, it may generate compelling evidence that the classic distinction between dorsal and ventral visual streams extends into the human prefrontal cortex.

Working on the project will entail reading relevant literature, collecting behavioural data, delivering TMS (after receiving training), and contributing to the analysis, interpretation, and presentation of results.

Project ID: Project 42- Paul Muhle-Karbe- 78- "A computational model of memory form..."
Project title: A computational model of memory formation and removal
Project summary:
Working memory describes the ability to maintain information that is no longer present in the environment. It provides a flexible mental workspace that scaffolds most higher cognitive functions. For a long time, a central objective in neuroscience has been to understand brain mechanisms that underpin working memory. This research has made great progress in revealing how the brain retains information, but it has neglected a key aspect: how are memories removed when they are no longer relevant for guiding behaviour?

Understanding removal mechanisms is important. Working memory only has a very small capacity, so efficient removal is critical to make optimal use of this mental workspace. Conversely, several mental health conditions are characterised by difficulties with removal (e.g., rumination in depression or intrusive thoughts in OCD), so understanding mechanisms behind removal may also inform better treatment to advance mental health.

This project will leverage computational modelling to interrogate how the human brain dynamically forms and dissolves memories for adaptive behaviour in a rapidly changing world.
Topic: working memory, removal,
Methodology:
This project will interrogate how the human brain adaptively removes memories. It will extend an existing computational model that provides an excellent fit to diverse brain recording data during memory maintenance (Manohar et al, 2019 – see seed references). We will equip the model with different removal mechanisms (implemented via spiking activity or synaptic plasticity), and examine its dynamics under different task demands. Careful simulations will be conducted to generate diagnostic experimental predictions to probe the contribution of each mechanism to memory removal in the human brain.

Working on the project will involve reading relevant literature, conducting simulations (under close supervision), and contributing to the interpretation of results. Depending on the student’s interest, the project may also involve testing some of the newly generated predictions via targeted behavioural experiments. The project will be carried out in close collaboration with Prof Sanjay Manohar at the University of Oxford.

Project title: Digital Consumption and Well-Being: The Role of Self-Control and Happiness

Project ID: Project 21- Romy Froemer- 53- "In the eye of the beholder's goal: n..."
Project title: In the eye of the beholder's goal: neural and computational mechanisms underpinning value-based choice
Project summary: From the choice of breakfast to the choice of romantic partner, value-based decisions permeate everyday life. Research has shown that these decisions are linked to people's attention: Options that are looked at more are more likely to be chosen. This robust empirical result has been taken as evidence that attention amplifies the value of options. However, more recent work suggests that the relationship is the other way around: The more people consider choosing an option, the more they will look at it, regardless of its value. Disrupting this choice-attention feedback loop reveals a separate, distinct effect of attention on choice that depends on people's expectations and how an options' value compares to them. In addition, research has show that people's choice behavior and gaze patterns are strongly influenced not by value per se, but by how values relate to the decision-maker's current goal. Taken together this work suggests that goals and attention jointly shape how people evaluate their options and ultimately choose. Here we will use attention and goal manipulations to test predictions of a model of this interaction and record EEG to shed new light on the underlying neural correlated of value-processing and decision-making.

Project ID: Project 3- Rory Devine- 49- "Childhood neurodiversity, mental hea..."

Project summary:
Emerging evidence indicates that children’s mental health is linked with both educational and social outcomes (e.g., Morris et al., 2021). The over-arching aim of this project is to examine the developmental impact of childhood mental health and neurodiversity on later social and educational outcomes.

The project uses existing data from a large-scale longitudinal study of approximately 8000 children tracked across four time points between ages 9 to 20 years. The dataset includes measures of children’s mental health, neurodiversity, cognitive ability, academic performance, educational attainment, and friendship and peer relationships. The dataset also contains rich information on the socio-demographic characteristics of participants and their families.

Project ID: Project 31- Sanne van der Kleij- 70- "Examining the factor structure and i..."
Project title: Examining the factor structure and internal validity of a feelings about literacy scale
Project summary:

Key to developing these reading skills is regular leisure time reading (Pfost et al., 2018). According to theory on reading engagement, founded in principles of self-determination theory (SDT, Ryan & Deci, 2000), development of reading motivation hinges on intrinsic and extrinsic factors (e.g. Conradi et al., 2014). It is also argued it’s not only our actual reading ability that is associated with how much we engage in reading and writing in our own time, but how we feel about our own reading and writing skills (e.g. our perceived competence) also determines whether we actually engage with these activities.
The purpose of the project is to explore the relationship between feelings about reading and writing, and whether this is associated with the amount of recreational reading and writing that adults engage in. This project aims to validate the factor structure and internal validity of a feelings about literacy scale, developed by adapting several previously published scales (i.e. Reading amount, adapted from Schutte & Malouff, 2007, affect, adapted from MacArthur et al. 2015, and self-efficacy, adapted from Carroll & Fox 2017; and writing amount, adapted from Schutte & Malouff, 2007, affect, adapted from MacArthur et al. 2015, self-efficacy, adapted from MacArthur et al. 2015).
The existing data set includes data from ~600 undergraduate students and includes data about demographic factors (e.g., age, gender, student status) and reading and writing frequency and self-competence.

Project ID: Project 51- Sarah Beck- 85- "Innovation, creativity, and problem ..."
Project title: Innovation, creativity, and problem solving
Project summary:
Imagine trying to rescue your keys that have fallen behind a radiator, perhaps you might use a ruler or a coat-hanger to try to reach them. Innovating a tool is a complex challenge that is likely to involve executive functions, creativity (such as divergent thinking), and imagination.
In this project we will look at adults' ability to flexibly innovate solutions to problems and the relationship between success on problem solving tasks and other cognitive and creativity measures. If students are interested it may be possible to explore the relation between these constructs and neurodiversity traits.

Project ID: Project 10- Sophie Sowden-Carvalho- 56- "Testing the Double Empathy Framework..."
Project title: Testing the Double Empathy Framework: Autistic and non-autistic communication of emotional experiences.
Project summary:
This study aims to investigate cross-neurotype emotional communication and empirically test the Double Empathy Framework. Using an online task, autistic and non-autistic adults will watch autistic and non-autistic narrators deliver emotional narratives and rate their emotions and first impressions of narrators. We would like to better understand predictors of communication and first impression success from these video stimuli and use this to inform an in-person, live interaction study. The live interaction study will be an opportunity for students to gain hands on experience in measuring subjective, behavioural and physiological synchrony between pairs of individuals of the same or different neurotypes.

The Double Empathy Framework suggests that autistic people experience social challenges due to a bi-directional breakdown in communication between two different minds (i.e. autistic and non-autistic). Empirical research into autistic people’s communication inspired by this framework has been mixed, with some studies finding an advantage for same-neurotype communication, while others suggest communication success does not neatly depend on dyad neurotype. Project ID: Project 14- Stacey Bissell- 60- "Reshaping behavioural Interventions ..."
Project title: Reshaping behavioural Interventions for Sleep in NeuroGenetic syndromes (RISING)
Project summary:
The prevalence of poor sleep is elevated in children with an intellectual disability compared to age-matched peers without neurodevelopmental conditions (Quine, 2001; Richdale, Francis, Gavidia-Payne, & Cotton, 2000). In children with an intellectual disability, estimates vary between 16-84%, with settling and waking problems being particularly common (Johnson, 1996; Quine, 1991; Wiggs & Stores, 1996). Co-occurring conditions that can exacerbate poor sleep, include: secondary health conditions resulting in pain (e.g. constipation, gastro-oesophageal reflux, respiratory tract infections, otitis media, dental caries), epilepsy (e.g. fragmented sleep architecture, abnormal EEG activity, the presence of nocturnal seizures, or the prescription of anti-epileptic medication), and co-occurring psychiatric diagnoses (e.g. anxiety, depression, sedatory side-effects of benzodiazepines). In addition, there are several neurogenetic syndrome groups where there are phenotypic physiological characteristics that are known to exacerbate poor sleep. For example, in Smith-Magenis syndrome loss of function or mutation to the retinoic acid-induced 1 gene (RAI1) affects circadian rhythms (DeLeersnyder et al., 2001; Potocki et al., 2000) resulting in an inverted melatonin release pattern and distinct sleep profile characterised by early morning waking and excessive daytime sleepiness. Physical facial features of Down syndrome confer risk for obstructive sleep apnoea (Lee et al.,2018; Trois et al., 2009), resulting in a distinct sleep profile of sleep disordered breathing.

First-line behavioural interventions focus on the promotion of good sleep hygiene practices (e.g. limited access to electronic devices before bed, a sleep-conducive environment and bedtime routine; Jan et al., 2008) and parent education to support a behavioural intervention approach, such as graduated extinction (Malow et al., 2012; Rigney et al., 2018). However, research into the efficacy of individualised targeted behavioural interventions (e.g. graduated extinction) for children with neurogenetic syndromes is virtually non-existent despite evident effectiveness in autism, ADHD and intellectual disability populations (Rigney et al., 2018). A move towards intervention is particularly important, given sleep problems in children with developmental delay predict the frequency and severity of daytime behaviours that challenge (e.g. aggression, overactivity; Adams, Matson, & Jang, 2014; Didden et al., 2002) and given the association between poor sleep and negative cognitive outcomes/executive functioning deficits in some neurogenetic syndrome groups (e.g. Joyce et al., 2020).

The main aim of the current study is to examine sleep and daytime outcomes in children with neurogenetic syndromes receiving tailored behavioural sleep interventions. Using subjective and objective measures of sleep (e.g. sleep questionnaires, sleep diaries, actigraphy) and daytime outcomes (e.g. behavioural questionnaires, executive functioning tasks), we will investigate changes in sleep following intervention and associations between sleep parameters and daytime outcomes. Parents/caregivers of children aged 4-15 years who meet eligibility criteria will be invited
to participate. Participants will complete baseline assessments prior to implementing a tailored sleep intervention. Following the intervention period, the same assessment battery will be re-administered to allow pre-post comparisons of child and main caregiver sleep, child daytime functioning outcomes and parent/caregiver wellbeing. In addition, qualitative interviews will be conducted with approximately 5-8 parents/caregivers following their involvement in the intervention, to explore perceptions of intervention acceptability and feasibility.

Methodology: pre-post quantitative analysis, qualitative analysis, actigraphy

Project ID: Project 6- Stephane De Brito- 52- "Psychopathy and brain correlates of ..."
Project title: Psychopathy and brain correlates of mate poaching
Project summary:
This project is a direct collaboration with colleagues at Kyoto University in Japan; regular contact with them will be necessary.

Purpose, background, and research questions

This research project explores how personality traits relate to behaviours around romantic attraction, specifically in situations where someone tries to attract a person who is already in a relationship — a behaviour known as "mate-poaching". While this behaviour is generally considered socially unacceptable, it happens fairly often in many cultures and may reflect different personal motivations.

The main part of the project will be a brain imaging (MRI) study with young adult men in the UK to investigate whether differences in brain activity — particularly in areas involved in decision-making and how we evaluate others — relate to people’s willingness to engage in mate-poaching. We are especially interested in whether brain responses explain the link between certain personality traits and this type of behaviour.

Hypotheses / research questions:

Which aspects of personality are most strongly linked to a tendency to pursue others who are already in relationships?

Are specific areas of brain activity or brain structures/network, especially in regions linked to evaluating others and making decisions, associated with interest in mate-poaching?

Can differences in brain responses or brain structure help explain why some men with higher levels of certain personality traits are more likely to engage in this behaviour?

Expected outcomes:

We expect to find that men who score higher on certain personality traits (e.g., impulsiveness, emotional coldness) report more frequent mate-poaching behaviour. We expect that men who show more interest in mate-poaching will also show stronger or more distinct brain activity in specific regions involved in decision-making. These brain patterns may help explain why some people are more likely to engage in this type of behaviour.
Topic: psychopathy, social relationships, neuroimaging
Methodology: In person testing using psychometric and MRI.

Project ID: Project 4- Suzanne Higgs - 48- "Effects of removing high fat high su..."
Project title: Effects of removing high fat high sugar foods on appetite and memory
Project summary: The proposed study will investigate whether cutting out foods high in fat and sugar (HFS) can improve brain function and appetite control in young adults who regularly consume these foods. Previous research suggests that even a short exposure to HFS foods can negatively affect memory, particularly memory processes linked to the hippocampus, a brain region important for learning and appetite regulation. Poor memory can make it harder to remember what has been eaten, leading to overeating and reduced feelings of fullness. This study addresses that gap by testing whether removing these foods from the diets of young, healthy, habitual consumers leads to measurable improvements in memory, appetite control, and other aspects of cognitive functioning. The findings could help identify a practical way to support both brain health and healthier eating habits early in life.

Project ID: Project 66- Tamara Swaab- 92- "How do meaningful gestures support l..."
Project title: How do meaningful gestures support language comprehension?
Project summary: Successful communication requires us to rapidly select and interpret words from among the thousands of words represented in our brains. This is a remarkable computational challenge that may be affected by increasing experience with more than one language. One way the brain makes comprehension more efficient is by using context to anticipate upcoming information. In face-to-face communication, that context comes not only from speech, but also from what we see: a speaker's facial movements and gestures can help us understand what is being said and may even allow us to predict what is coming next. Project ID: Project 47- Wieske van Zoest- 82- "Visual cues in attention..."
Project title: Visual cues in attention
Project summary:
Humans are remarkably sensitive to the spatial cues around them, from a simple arrow or the word “LEFT” to the subtle shift of someone’s gaze or the direction of a pointing hand. These visual cues act like silent guides, steering our attention and helping us react more quickly and accurately to what’s happening in our surroundings. But not everyone responds to these cues in the same way. Factors like gender, dominance, race, emotional state, neurodiversity, and cognitive load shape how we interpret and act on these signals.

Moreover, not all cues are created equal: while some, like gaze direction, tap into largely automatic processes, others such as symbolic arrows rely on learned associations and may engage different cognitive processes. Additionally, it turns out that these visual cues don’t operate in isolation. They often interact with sounds and other sensory input, creating complex, cross-modal effects that further influence perception.

This research project aims to uncover how and why people process visual cues differently, and what this reveals about the hidden biases shaping our perception.
Topic: Visual attention, cognition, individual differences
Methodology: Behavioural methods (like reaction time), questionnaires, possibly eye movements
